primer.intro: A binary tree is the first structure where recursion stops being optional. Every node holds a value and two children, left and right, each of which is itself a binary tree - possibly empty. That self-similarity means most tree algorithms are three lines long: handle the empty tree, recurse on both children, combine the results at the root. The topic's vocabulary is the traversals. The three depth-first orders - preorder, inorder, postorder - differ only in when the root is visited relative to its two subtrees, and breadth-first level order walks the tree floor by floor with a queue. Learn to read a tree from its level-order description, with -1 for absent children, because that is how every problem here hands you its input.
whenToUse: The data is hierarchical: nested structure, filesystems, expression shapes.
Every node must be visited once in a discipline - pick the traversal whose visit moment matches the job.
A property of the whole tree reduces to the same property of the two subtrees plus constant work at the root.
The question is level-by-level - widths, floors, the shallowest something - which calls for the queue.
primer.mentalModel: Trust the subtree - the same leap of faith as plain recursion. The depth of a tree is 1 plus the larger of its two subtree depths; two trees are identical when their roots match and both subtree pairs are identical; the empty tree answers every base case for free. For the depth-first orders, place the root-visit: before both recursions is preorder, between them is inorder, after both is postorder - the names literally say where the root goes. Level order is different machinery: a queue seeded with the root, where each served node enqueues its children, so the queue always holds a slice of one or two adjacent levels. The recursion stack costs the tree's height; the queue costs the tree's widest level.
mistakes: Skipping the empty-tree base case, then dereferencing a missing child one level down.
Mixing depth-in-nodes with depth-in-edges - a lone node is depth 1 in one convention, 0 in the other; fix it first.
Comparing two trees by comparing traversal outputs - different shapes can print the same sequence.

example.title: Maximum depth by trusting the subtrees
example.explain: The empty tree contributes 0, and every real node adds 1 on top of its taller subtree - that single sentence is the whole algorithm. The work per node is constant, so the run is linear, and the deepest chain of open calls equals the tree's height. The identical-trees check wears the same skeleton with two pointers in lockstep: both empty is yes, exactly one empty is no, and otherwise the values must match and both subtree pairs must agree.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Preorder Traversal - the three depth-first orders are one function with a single line moved, and seeing that is the lesson.

sections.title: Three traversals, one function
sections.text: Write the recursion once: recurse left, recurse right, and a visit line you slide into one of three slots. Visit first and you get preorder - the order that copies or serialises a tree, because every root is announced before its contents. Visit between and you get inorder - on search trees this emits sorted order, a fact the next topic leans on heavily. Visit last and you get postorder - children are finished before their parent, which is the only safe order for computing subtree sizes or tearing a tree down. When someone hands you a traversal puzzle, locate the root in the output: at the front it was preorder, at the back postorder, somewhere in the middle inorder.

check.prompt: A tree has root 1, left child 2 and right child 3. What does its inorder traversal print?

options.explain: Inorder is left subtree, root, right subtree - the root lands in the middle.
Root first is preorder, the copying order.
Root last is postorder, the children-first order.
That visits the right subtree before the left - none of the three orders do.

reveal.solution: Inorder recurses into the left subtree first, then visits the root, then recurses right. The left subtree is the lone node 2, so it prints first; the root 1 follows; the right subtree 3 closes: 2 1 3. Move the visit line to the front of the function and the same tree prints 1 2 3 (preorder); move it to the back and it prints 2 3 1 (postorder).

sections.title: Floor by floor
sections.text: Level order trades the call stack for an explicit queue. Seed it with the root; then repeatedly serve a node, record its value, and enqueue its children. Because children join at the back while parents leave from the front, the queue never mixes more than two adjacent levels, and freezing the queue's length at the top of a round tells you exactly how many nodes the current level holds - the key to per-level answers like widths and rightmost views. The queue's peak size is the tree's widest level, which in a bushy tree approaches half the nodes; the recursion stack of the depth-first orders costs the height instead. Pick the traversal whose memory bill matches your tree's shape.

quiz.prompt: Every node must learn the size of its own subtree. Which traversal order does the job?

options.text: Postorder - both children finish before the parent combines their sizes
options.explain: Size at a node is 1 plus the two child sizes, so children must report first.
The parent is visited before the children's sizes exist.
The right subtree is still unvisited when the root is processed.
Parents are served before children - exactly backwards for this.

quiz.prompt: Serialise a tree so it can be rebuilt exactly. Which order is the natural choice?

options.text: Preorder with explicit markers for absent children
options.explain: Each root is announced before its contents, so rebuilding peels values off the front.
Many different trees share one inorder; the shape is lost.
The markers are what pin the shape; dropping them loses it.
Sorting erases the structure entirely.

quiz.prompt: Find the shallowest node satisfying some property. Which traversal guarantees the first hit is shallowest?

options.text: Level order - it visits all of depth d before anything at depth d+1
options.explain: Breadth-first order makes the first match automatically the shallowest.
Depth-first dives to the bottom of the left side before touching depth 2 elsewhere.
It starts reporting from the deepest leaves - the opposite end.
Depth plays no role in inorder's sequence.

quiz.prompt: Decide whether two trees are exactly the same. Which plan is sound?

options.text: Walk both in lockstep: both empty yes, one empty no, match values, recurse on both pairs
options.explain: Structure and values are checked together at every position.
Different shapes can share an inorder - the sequence underdetermines the tree.

options.text: Compare their depths and node counts
options.explain: Two different trees can agree on both numbers.

options.text: Compare the sums of their values
options.explain: Sums collide constantly; they certify nothing.

quiz.prompt: For the tree built from 1 2 3 4 5 -1 -1 (level order, -1 absent), what does postorder print?

options.explain: Left subtree bottom-up (4, 5, then 2), right subtree (3), root last.
Root first is preorder.
Root in the middle is inorder.
Floor by floor is level order.

quiz.prompt: The entries 3 2 -1 1 -1 build a left-leaning chain. What does level order print?

options.explain: Each level holds one node: 3, then 2, then 1.
That is this chain's inorder - deepest first.
The queue serves 2 before its child 1 joins.
The root always leads in level order.

quiz.prompt: Depth in nodes of the tree built from 1 2 3 4 5 -1 -1?

options.explain: The chain 1, 2, 4 (or 1, 2, 5) holds three nodes.
That counts edges on the longest chain, the other convention.
Five is the node count; depth follows one chain only.
Depth 1 is a lone root; this tree has grandchildren.

quiz.prompt: A depth-first traversal of n nodes costs how much time and stack?

options.text: Linear time, stack proportional to the height
options.explain: Each node is visited once; open calls line up along one root-to-leaf path.

options.text: Linear time, stack proportional to n always
options.explain: Only a degenerate chain costs n stack; bushy trees cost log n.
No sorting happens - each node is touched a constant number of times.
Quadratic needs re-visiting; traversal visits once.

quiz.prompt: What is level order's peak extra memory on a bushy tree of n nodes?

options.text: About n/2 - the widest level sits in the queue at once
options.explain: A full bottom level of a complete tree holds roughly half the nodes.
The queue grows with the widest level, which grows with n.
Height is the depth-first stack bill; the queue holds widths.
Served nodes leave the queue; it holds at most two adjacent levels.

quiz.prompt: This depth function returns 0 for every tree. What is the bug?

options.text: The node itself is uncounted - return 1 plus the max of the child depths
options.explain: Without the +1 every path reports the base case's 0 all the way up.

options.text: Math.max is the problem; use Math.min
options.explain: Depth wants the taller subtree; min computes the shallowest leaf instead.
That patches a lone root but counts every absent child as a level.
Depth is symmetric; swapping changes nothing.

quiz.prompt: This identical-trees check says yes for trees of different shapes. Why?

options.text: One inorder fits many shapes - compare structure recursively, in lockstep
options.explain: A left chain and a right chain of the same values print the same inorder.
Closer, but still ambiguous unless absent children are marked.
The strings compare fine; they just encode too little.
Even a perfect inorder underdetermines the tree - the idea is the flaw.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for any tree routine here?

options.explain: Both children absent at the root - every base case and the depth convention fire at once.
Pleasant, but it avoids the boundary paths.
Value magnitude flows through untouched.
Traversals report positions; duplicates change nothing structural.
